title: Seven times a day (ch. 16)
hookLine: the monks pray seven times a day, as the psalm says
tomorrow: Nothing before the work of God (ch. 43)

lines: SEVEN TIMES A DAY I HAVE GIVEN PRAISE.
cards: "Seven times a day I have given praise to thee." A line from a psalm, the hundred and eighteenth by the Douay-Rheims numbering: a poet writing about how much he loves God's law.
It reads like a figure of speech, the way someone says they've told you a thousand times. Saint Benedict didn't read it as a figure of speech.
He read it as a schedule, and in chapter sixteen of his Rule he builds the whole monastery's day on it.

teach.h: THE PSALM SAYS SEVEN. BENEDICT SAYS WHEN.
teach.b: You met the Church's clock back on day two hundred forty; here is Benedict's version. Chapter sixteen is short and practical.
The prophet says seven times a day, Benedict writes, and we keep that sacred number if we pray at these hours: Lauds, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers and Compline.
Lauds at dawn, Vespers toward evening, Compline before sleep, and the others spaced through the working day.

teach.h: AND AT MIDNIGHT, THE NIGHT OFFICE.
teach.b: The same psalm also speaks of rising at midnight to give praise, so the monks rise in the night too, for the night office. Two lines from one psalm, and the whole day and night is mapped.
That arrangement of prayer has a name: the Divine Office. The monks don't wait until they feel like praying.

teach.h: A DUTY, SUNG MOSTLY IN PSALMS.
teach.b: The bell rings, they gather, and they pray mostly the psalms, aloud, together, verse answering verse across the choir. What does it do to a day? A day without anchors tends to run in one long blur from alarm to pillow.

teach.h: THE DAY CUT INTO PIECES BY PRAYER.
teach.b: A day with set hours is cut into pieces, like a field divided by hedges, with God at every gate. Nobody has to invent the words; the psalms supply them.
And when a monk is tired or distracted, the hour comes anyway and carries him. The Church still prays the hours, now usually called the Liturgy of the Hours.
Priests and religious pray it, and lay Catholics are invited to join, at home, on the bus, with a book or an app.

how: Catholic priests and religious pray the Liturgy of the Hours daily, and some lay Catholics pray Morning and Evening Prayer from a breviary or an app; Benedictine communities gather in choir for the hours through the day.

games.q: you're Benedict. your psalm says seven times a day I praise you, and also, I rose at midnight to praise you. how do you set the monastery's day?
o: seven hours of prayer by day, and rising at night as well.
one long prayer at dawn that counts for all seven.
seven times in total, with one of them at midnight.
games.why: Benedict keeps both lines: seven day hours, from Lauds to Compline, and the night office besides.

practice: Look at the shape of the day ahead and choose three anchors: one near waking, one somewhere in the middle, one near sleep, and picture where you'll be at each.
A minute is all each one needs: if you pray, a line from a psalm or the Our Father; if you don't, three slow breaths and a look at where you are.
